newsitem.title: USA: US corporate bond players return to firm market.
newsitem.headline: US corporate bond players return to firm market.

text.p: The U.S. corporate bond market started its first full week of the new year on a strong note, as investors bought a fair amount of investment-grade corporate bonds on Monday, market sources said.

"Spreads in (high-grade) bonds are marginally tighter as a result of good retail activity," said one trader. "People who were on the sidelines at the end of last year are putting money back to work today."
Prices in the junk market were unchanged on light trading volume as investors focused primarily on the growing forward calendar of new junk deals, traders said.
Among new issues, Commonwealth Edison, a unit of Unicom Corp, sold $300 million in debt via Salomon Brothers Inc.
The utility's two-part offering priced very aggressively due to strong investor demand, traders said.
The 7.735 percent seven-year notes were priced at 98 basis points over Treasuries, while the 7.625 percent 10-year notes priced at 112 basis points over.

Among individual credits, Raytheon Company's outstanding 10-year debt widened to 60 from 55 basis points over Treasuries on news of the company's $2.95 billion bid for the defense assets of Texas Instruments Inc.
Moody's Investors Service placed Raytheon's A1-rated debt under review for a possible downgrade as a result of the additional leverage the company would take on if the acquisition is completed.

In the junk bond market, Apple Computer Inc's $300 million in senior notes dropped five points in morning trading after the company announced it expects to take a $100 million to $150 million loss due to poor demand for its computer products.
Traders said the bonds dropped to 82-84 bid from 87-88 bid in the morning and rallied to 84 1/2-86 levels by midday.
Elsewhere, Levitz Furniture Inc's 9.625 percent notes due 2003 gained over three points on Monday, ahead of the company's release tomorrow of same-store sales figures for December, said traders.
"I would presume that someone has some insight into what the numbers will be," said one Wall Street retail sector analyst.
"Back in December, the company indicated that same-store sales were coming along nicely and that they were expecting positive results for the months," he added.
But Gary Miller, Levitz's assistant treasurer, denied the company had made any comments about its December figures.
"I can only speculate that someone else is speculating on it. We have put nothing out and will have nothing out until tomorrow," Miller said.
Returning to the broader markets, high-grade corporate bond spreads ended the day one to two basis points tighter across the board.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury closed at 96-16/32 to yield 6.77 percent. The price was down 16/32 from yesterday's close.
